newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Philippine government, rebels edge towards peace.
newsitem.headline: Philippine government, rebels edge towards peace.

text.p: The Philippine government and an exiled rebel leader signed a statement on Monday agreeing to push for the completion of peace negotiations by the end of June, a spokesman said on Monday.

Officials from the Philippine government, including Speaker of the Philippines' House of Representatives Jose de Venecia, earlier met exiled Communist rebels in a luxury Amsterdam hotel in a bid to breathe new life into the peace process.

Mike Genovea, media director for the speaker's office, said De Venecia had signed a joint declaration with Jose Maria Sison, Chief Political Consultant of the National Democratic Front of the Philippines (NDFP).
He said the men had held two rounds of successful informal talks in Amsterdam in an effort to boost the formal peace negotiations between the Philippines government and the NDFP.

"The two sides have agreed to exert utmost efforts to complete negotiations on or before June 30, 1997, which is also the target date for the Philippine exit from the restrictive controls of the International Monetary Fund," the joint statement said.

It said the parties agreed that the current negoations were aimed at defining the basis of "a just and lasting peace" and referred to economic reforms aimed at wiping out mass poverty and delivering basic social services to poor provinces.

"Sison said that the people's demands for national and social emancipation and all-round development must be satisfied and that the root causes of the armed conflict between the Government and the NDFP must be addressed," it added.

Peace talks between the two sides conducted in the Dutch city of Utrecht, where Sison lives in exile, have run into difficulties over the government panel's refusal to acknowledge human rights violations, Sison said in a statement issued before Monday's meeting.

"The (government) negotiating panel...deny the perpetration of human rights violations even under the Marcos regime," the statement said. As a result the government-NDFP negotiations had run into "serious difficulties".

The NDFP further charges the government with obstructing claims by victims of human rights abuses to Swiss-held assets in accounts opened by former Philippine dictator Ferdinand Marcos, who ruled the country for 14 years until he was overthrown in a 1986 popular revolt.

Insurgents have been operating in the Philippines since 1969. The military says their strength has fallen to around 5,000 from a peak of more than 26,000 in the late 1980s because of the collapse of communism in Europe, battlefield losses and the surrender of many followers.
